entries.title: FIFA plans to form new commercial subsidiary and sell stake
entries.summary: FIFA has announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary and to sell a non-controlling interest to private investors. It needs approval from member associations, but is claiming that it will benefit them financially.
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

FIFA has announced plans to form a commercial subsidiary and to sell a non-controlling interest to private investors. It needs approval from member associations, but is claiming that it will benefit them financially.

FIFA plans to create a new commercial subsidiary valued at $20 billion (roughly €17.5 billion) and sell non-controlling minority stakes to investors, world football's governing body announced on Tuesday. 

It called on its 211 member federations to back the plan, saying that if they voted in favor they "would benefit immediately from increased funding."

As soon as the news emerged, European football federation UEFA issued fierce criticism of the plan, saying it "crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross."

The push comes immediately after this summer's World Cup hosted primarily in the US, with FIFA listing a series of potential investors and advisors from the country. Infantino's close relationship with US President Donald Trump had already prompted criticism in some corners prior to Tuesday's announcement, which came a day after Infantino issued a fiery statement defending the tournament in the US and the controversies that accompanied it. 

What did FIFA say about the plan?

FIFA said that it planned to set up a "new FIFA-owned and controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA's commercial and event operations" that it would call the FIFA Forward Enterprise, or FFE.

It said this company would be valued at $20 billion and that FFE would aim to raise up to $4.2 billion "this year" by "carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FFE."

FIFA claimed that "all net benefits of FFE will be reinvested back into football worldwide," without clarifying what constituted "net benefits," or what gains investors then stood to make.

FFE would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts, the statement said. By far the most valuable of these for FIFA are those connected to the World Cup, although other competitions like the recently and controversially relaunched FIFA Club World Cup also apply. 

Ahead of this month's World Cup final in New York, FIFA President Gianni Infantino had told member associations that he wanted to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity" of the organization.

Infantino tried to portray the changes as seeking to more evenly spread out football funding and to "democratize" the game, seemingly in a pitch aimed at less wealthy (and more numerous) football associations in particular.

"As its global governing body, FIFA is responsible for making sure the game reaches every corner of the world, and that the value it creates supports federations and communities everywhere. Our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world," Infantino said in FIFA's press release.

"We intend to invest heavily even in the smallest or most remote parts of the footballing world, places that are too often passed over," Infantino said, championing the new investment scheme dubbed the FIFA Fast Forward Programme, or FFFP.

How did UEFA react?

FIFA's press release was published soon after an article on the website of UK newspaper The Times — followed soon after by the Financial Times, Bloomberg and others — began attracting international attention.

The European football federation UEFA issued a scathing response online soon after the news broke.

"This crosses a line that football's governing insitutions should never cross," it said. "UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments, and everyone who cares about the future of the game."

UEFA said that the "soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially."

UEFA and FIFA have clashed repeated in recent months and years under Infantino's stewardship, including during the World Cup this summer.

"None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA argued.

UEFA, however, only represents around one quarter of FIFA's member associations, so its opposition is by no means guaranteed to halt the plan.

What do we know about the proposed investors and advisors?

FIFA said its structure would be similar to "other sports governing bodies with dedicated commercial subsidiaries," and said that investors would be selected "against clear long-term, governance and strategic criteria."

It described ideal investors as long-term partners who could contribute capital and commercial expertise to help FIFA's goal of growing the game.

"Subject to these final agreements and required approvals, Thrive Eternal, a permanent capital holding company, is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE," FIFA said, referring to the holding company set up this year by Joshua Kushner, brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior negotiator Jared Kushner.

Infantino's relations with Trump came under scrutiny more than once amid the World Cup process — perhaps most notably when FIFA overturned the red card suspension of US striker Folarin Balogun ahead of defeat against Belgium, and when Donald Trump was given the inaugural "FIFA Peace Prize" in a much-mocked event last December. This came weeks before the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and then the war with Iran. 

FIFA also said that Greg Maffei, the CEO of BANN Ventures and formerly "the CEO of Liberty Media during its acquisition and ownership of Formula 1" motor racing, "has been a key commercial advisor and will remain involved in the establishment of FFE in this next phase."

It said that investment bank JP Morgan was engaged to work alongside FIFA, and Rome-based economic consulting firm OpenEconomic were also "engaging with prospective long-term investors."

FIFA said that it was trying to set up a geographically diversified investor group and said it had received expressions of interest from every major region in the world.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Germany: Low Rhine River levels could push economy into stagnation
entries.summary: Record-low water levels on the Rhine are forcing cargo vessels to run with sharply reduced loads, driving up transport costs. Economists warn the disruption could wipe out Germany's already weak summer growth.
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

Record-low water levels on the Rhine are forcing cargo vessels to run with sharply reduced loads, driving up transport costs. Economists warn the disruption could wipe out Germany's already weak summer growth.

Persistently low water levels on the Rhine River could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy said on Tuesday.

Prolonged dry weather has continued to lower levels on the busiest inland trade waterway on Europe, connecting the vast port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany. 

Less rain fell than forecast this past weekend, and the national weather service now forecasts another incoming period of high temperatures, particularly further south along the river.

How can a low Rhine affect the economy?

The Rhine carries key commodities including grain, minerals, ores, coal and petroleum products such as petrol.

When the river is low, cargo vessels can no longer travel fully loaded and must spread shipments across several ships.

Traders have said some inland vessels are operating at only 15% to 20% of their maximum load. That raises transport costs and places further pressure on an economy that had recently begun to show signs of a modest recovery.

Many economists expect growth of no more than 0.2% during the summer months, meaning the disruption could push Europe's largest economy toward stagnation.

"The effects could be strong enough to reduce gross domestic product in the third quarter by 0.1% to 0.2%," Stefan Kooths, director of the institute's business cycle and growth research group, told the Reuters news agency.

At Kaub, a crucial bottleneck between the cities of Koblenz and Mainz, a benchmark measurement gauge fell to 30 centimeters (12 inches) on Tuesday. Germany's waterways authority expects it to drop to around 25 centimeters by Friday, matching a record low reached in October 2018.

"As water levels are unlikely to rise suddenly above the critical threshold at the beginning of August, transport capacity is likely to remain impaired for some time next month," Kooths said.

Poor economy could lessen impact

Under normal economic conditions, the prolonged disruption would reduce industrial activity by around 0.8% in July and cut overall monthly economic output by about 0.2%, Kooths said.

However, the current weakness of German industry could make the overall impact somewhat smaller. 

Deutsche Bank Research analysts warned that the problem was being compounded by the months-long closure of an important rail alternative.

The railway line on the eastern bank of the Rhine is closed to freight traffic for renovation work until December 12. Even under normal circumstances, rail can replace only a limited share of inland shipping capacity.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Fact check: Berlin Pride attack claims debunked
entries.summary: Following the Islamist terrorist attack at Berlin Pride, rumors, false claims and misleading videos have been spreading on social media. DW Fact check examines some of the most widely shared claims.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Berlin Pride attack claims debunked

July 28, 2026

Following the Islamist terrorist attack at Berlin Pride, rumors, false claims and misleading videos have been spreading on social media. DW Fact check examines some of the most widely shared claims.

In the aftermath of Saturday's attack at Berlin's Christopher Street Day, which is how the city's LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations are known, more and more details have emerged about the alleged perpetrator and the attack itself.

But as it is often the case in the aftermath of such events, verified information can be hard to come by, while rumors and false claims spread rapidly on social media.

DW Fact check takes a look at several of such viral posts.

Toronto shooting falsely shared in connection with Berlin attack

Claim: A videoshared on TikTok shows a crowd of people fleeing from something happening off screen. Text overlaid on the video in the style of a location tag suggests that it shows Christopher Street Day (CSD) celebrations in Berlin. The video is circulating on various platforms and in multiple languages.

DW Fact check: False

The video does not show the attack on Berlin's Pride event that German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has classified as an "Islamist terrorist attack." 

A reverse image search leads to an older video on YouTubethat was published on July 13, 2026, well before the Berlin Pride celebrations.

The footage actually shows a shooting at a salsa festival in Toronto, Canada, on July 11. At least two people reportedly exchanged gunfire during the Salsa on St. Clair festival. 

According to statements by Canadian police,two people were killed. At least five others were injured. So far, Canadian police have not released any information about the motive behind the shooting.

The video has no connection to the attack in Berlin.

Does footage show the arrest of the suspected perpetrator?

Claim: Shaky nighttime footage shows a person in a white T-shirt lying on the ground with hands bound behind their back, while people in police uniforms stand nearby. According to some posts, such as this one on X,this six-second clip allegedly shows police arresting the suspected perpetrator at the scene of the attack. The claim is also circulating in Arabic, Hebrew and Russian.

DW Fact check: False

The video does not show the arrest of the suspected perpetrator. It was already circulating on social media shortly after the attack during the night from Saturday to Sunday.

At that time, however, the suspect was still on the run. The first reports that police had shot the alleged perpetrator did not emerge until more than 20 hours after the attack.

How did the video spread?

The media outlet Junge Freiheit initially shared the video on its social media channels, from where it was picked up by other accounts. The red-and-white "JF" logo is clearly visible in the video. Junge Freiheit is a right-wing German weekly newspaper.

In its Facebook post,Junge Freiheit initially wrote: "Arrest at the scene of the Berlin attack. It is still unclear whether this is the perpetrator." 

The outlet later updated the post with the clarification: "According to police, this is not the suspect. The suspect remains at large."

On X, Junge Freiheit originally wrote:"According to eyewitnesses, the man lying on the ground is the rampage driver arrested at CSD Berlin." 

The newspaper later deleted the post and disclosed that, according to police, the footage showed a different arrest on the sidelines of the CSD.

Whether the video was actually recorded in connection with the CSD in Berlin remains unclear. So far, there is no indication that the footage is older and therefore being taken out of context.

When asked whether the video showed a police operation related to the CSD, Berlin police neither confirmed nor denied that such an operation had taken place and referred inquiries to Germany's federal public prosecutor's office.

What is clear, however, is that the video does not show the arrest of the suspect.

AI videos pushing emotional CSD statements

Claim:  A numberof videoshave popped up on TikTok, allegedly showing genuine reactions to the Islamist terror attack in Berlin.

DW Fact check: Fake

The videos were generated using artificial intelligence. Their visual style makes this clear, and the platforms on which they appear also label them as AI-generated. Nevertheless, they are being widely shared in connection with Berlin Pride.

In one video, styled as a street interview, an AI-generated young woman draped in a rainbow flag says: "We just want to celebrate in peace." A voice from behind responds: "Enjoy what you voted for."

Another videostatement claims that the German government can no longer cope with Islamist terrorism.

The videos do not show real statements from CSD attendees. Instead, they present staged political messages designed to create the impression of authentic reactions to a real event.

Although clearly labeled as AI, such videos can still contribute to the spread of disinformation by associating real groups of people with political statements.

Users are also reacting to the AI-generated videos. Comments show people sharing blue heart emojis, a symbol associated with the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD), or writing comments such as: "Then you should have voted for the decent party."

The accountsharing these fake CSD reactions regularly shares AI-generated videos, some of them featuring political messages.

Another clip even imitates an official police statement,featuring an AI-generated police officer that claims that the suspected attacker was known to authorities but was repeatedly released because prisons were overcrowded.

Labels indicating AI-generated content are often small and can easily be overlooked while scrolling on mobile phone screens.

Note: This article is part of a collaboration between Germany's public broadcasting fact-checking teams ARD-Faktenfinder and DW Fact check.

The article was originally published in German.

entries.title: EU civil protection mechanism: Coordinating Europe's firefighters
entries.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has activated the EU civil protection mechanism to help combat devastating wildfires. The system has become increasingly effective, yet it will reach its limits in the summer of 2026.
entries.content:
France

EU civil protection mechanism: help with fighting wildfires

July 28, 2026

French President Emmanuel Macron has activated the EU civil protection mechanism to help combat devastating wildfires. The system has become increasingly effective, yet it will reach its limits in the summer of 2026.

France is quite well-prepared for wildfires. The government operates 12 Canadair water bombers and eight Dash firefighting aircraft. In addition, leased aircraft and helicopters are being used.

However, the fleet is currently needed simultaneously across many parts of the country. A drought has been intensifying for weeks, and several heat waves with temperatures sometimes exceeding 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) have left the vegetation extremely parched. The devastating wildfire near Bordeaux on the Atlantic coast has already engulfed more than 42,000 hectares of forest and vegetation.

At the same time, fires and follow-up extinguishing efforts in southern and southeastern France are tying up additional emergency personnel. In many places, firefighters are battling the flames in an exhausting, round-the-clock effort. However, strong winds are fanning the fire fronts, making them almost unstoppable, and more than 220,000 people have had to leave their homes and vacation homes so far.

The gravity of the situation is also underscored by the fact that the French government has deployed an A400M military transport aircraft equipped for aerial firefighting for the first time. The A400M can drop around 20 metric tons of fire retardant, more than three times as much as a Canadair.

Nevertheless, the situation is currently so dire that President Emmanuel Macron also activated the EU civil protection mechanism (CPM) and requested assistance from other European countries.

24/7 service at the emergency response coordination centre

To activate the CPM, a country reports its needs to the European Union's emergency response coordination centre, ERCC, in Brussels. ERCC experts assess which of the 37 participating countries can provide assistance.

Initial assistance for France was mobilized within a few hours and has since been significantly expanded. Firefighting aircraft and helicopters from Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Germany, Turkey, Sweden and Slovakia are supporting France, primarily in the greater Bordeaux area.

At the same time, however, the EU also dispatched six additional firefighting aircraft from Greece, Turkey and Italy to Spain. This means that 13 of the 22 firefighting aircraft available for this summer have already been mobilized for these two countries. The figures also demonstrate how quickly the European reserve can be drawn upon when multiple large-scale wildfires occur simultaneously. According to the European Commission, the resources currently available are therefore likely insufficient to keep pace with the scale of the fires.

Turkey, Norway and others cooperate with EU members

Since the launch of the civil protection mechanism in 2001, the system has been expanded several times. Since 2019, the EU has also launched rescEU, a strategic reserve comprising firefighting aircraft, medical equipment, field hospitals and specialized technology for chemical or nuclear emergencies. In addition to the 27 EU member states, 10 other countries are also participating in the civil protection mechanism, including Norway, Turkey and several Western Balkan states.

For the summer of 2026, Brussels also pre-positioned 777 firefighters from 14 countries in particularly vulnerable regions of France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Cyprus. The firefighting aircraft and helicopters of the European reserve are distributed across twelve countries and can be mobilized through the coordination center in Brussels. In addition, firefighting efforts are supported by high-resolution satellite imagery from the EU's Copernicus Earth observation program.

The heart of this cooperation is that one country may be able to spare aircraft or emergency personnel while another urgently needs them. However, the European principle of solidarity reaches its limits in situations where multiple countries are simultaneously affected by extreme weather events, which are likely to occur with increasing frequency due to climate change. In such cases, governments must weigh how much support they can send abroad without jeopardizing their own operational capacity.

Currently, Italy is battling wildfires within its own borders, even though it has not yet activated the mechanism. The European Commission expects an unusually long wildfire season this year. The mechanism was first activated at the end of April and could remain in effect until as late as early November.

Plans for a separate 'EU firefighting fleet'

The current European air reserve for fighting wildfires consists primarily of nationally operated aircraft that are committed as EU resources for a specific period. Meanwhile, the EU is establishing a rescEU fleet — permanently available and fully funded by EU resources — at a cost of approximately €600 million ($682m).

The plan is to acquire twelve new firefighting aircraft, which will be stationed in France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece and Croatia. The aircraft will be operated by the respective member states, but decisions regarding their deployment within the rescEU framework will be made jointly by the European Commission and the participating countries.

Wildfire prevention is key

Europe's wildfire response force can save time in an emergency and relieve the strain on national disaster response teams. However, according to the European Commission, this cannot compensate for a lack of wildfire prevention measures such as the creation of firebreaks and stricter building regulations in high-risk areas.

Furthermore, firefighting aircraft are most effective when fires are detected early. Once fire fronts measuring several kilometers have formed due to heat and strong winds, even additional aircraft from the European Union can often only contain the flames, but not fully extinguish them.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Poland: Top court rejects recognizing EU same-sex marriages
entries.summary: Poland's constitutional court has overturned plans to recognize same-sex marriages that took place in other EU member states. This defies an order from the EU's top court and could set up a clash on the matter.
entries.content:
Poland

Poland: Top court rejects recognizing EU same-sex marriages

July 28, 2026

Poland's constitutional court has overturned plans to recognize same-sex marriages that took place in other EU member states. This defies an order from the EU's top court and could set up a clash on the matter.

Poland's highest court, the Constitutional Tribunal on Tuesday overturned a law that would have led to the legal recognition of same-sex spouses who married in other EU member states and subsequently moved to Poland. 

The government in Warsaw had been moving to accommodate a ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union saying that majority-Catholic Poland, which does not permit same-sex marriage domestically, must at least recognize unions contracted elsewhere in the EU.

The unanimous ruling could set up a power struggle between Poland's top court and that of the 27-member bloc.

What did Poland's Constitutional Tribunal rule?

The court said in a statement on Tuesday that the judgment was unanimous and final and that EU same-sex marriages could not be copied into the country's civil registry as previously planned. 

It said that the plans for the "preparation and issuance of certified copies concerning unions contracted abroad that do not constitute a union between a woman and a man," were "inconsistent with Article 92, Paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 18 of the Constitution of the Republic of Poland."

Article 18 of the constitution reads as follows: "Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland."

In other words it both designates marriage as heterosexual in nature and as part of Poland's jurisdiction.

Article 92, Paragraph 1 meanwhile states that regulations should be specified by "the organs specified in the Constitution."

The court did not elaborate on its reasoning in its short statement, but this seemed to suggest its judges found that the European court order encroached on Poland's authority to set its family and marriage policies.

What had been previously agreed, when, and why?

The November 2025 ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union had not demanded that Poland legalize gay marriage, nor even that it recognize same-sex spouses as such legally. 

It did, however, demand that a same-sex couple who married legally elsewhere in the EU and then exercised "their freedom of movement to move and reside" in another state, like Poland, should have their marital status copied into the civil register if that was the only way to secure the benefits and securities of marital status in that country.

The case was initiated by two men, a Polish national and a German-Polish dual national, who had married legally while living in Germany in 2018 and then moved to Poland the following year.

Poland's Supreme Administrative Court had ruled in March that this step "does not violate national identity," nor interfere with Poland's authority to determine its own family and marriage laws.

Poland's government subsequently implemented the legislation in May, and it had been set to come into force as of the end of August.

But the right-wing opposition PiS party challenged the move at the Constitutional Tribunal, successfully as it transpires.

Poland's Constitutional Tribunal and the top EU courts have clashed before, not least in a long-running dispute over the contentious appointment of new judges to the court when PiS was in government, with the most recent European Court of Justice rebuke of Poland's top court being issued last December. 

Poland, with roughly 70% of the population identifying as Roman Catholic in census data, is one of just four EU members not to permit either same-sex marriages or same-sex civil unions, along with Bulgaria, Romania and Slovakia.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Could US airstrikes stop insurgency in Mali?
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump is considering airstrikes against the Al-Qaeda-linked JNIM in Mali, according to multiple reports. Analysts say such attacks might weaken the jihadists but would not address the core issues.
entries.content:
Mali

Could US airstrikes stop insurgency in Mali?

July 28, 2026

US President Donald Trump is considering airstrikes against the Al-Qaeda-linked JNIM in Mali, according to multiple reports. Analysts say such attacks might weaken the jihadists but would not address the core issues.

For years,Mali has struggled to contain a growing jihadist insurgency, particularly in the country's northern region. Following the withdrawal of French troops and despite the authorities' close cooperation with Russia, theal-Qaeda-linked Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) continues to expand its influence. Now, a new actor could enter the conflict: the United States (US).

Founded in 2017, JNIM unites several Islamist groups under the banner of al-Qaeda. Over the past years, the organization has developed into the most powerful jihadist force in the Sahel. Its objective is the establishment of an Islamist order and the displacement of state structures as well as Western influence.

"We are no longer talking about a group that only carries out isolated attacks," explains Tobias Rüttershof, head of the Sahel Program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation (KAS), which is affiliated with Germany's CDU party and has an office in Mali, in an interview with DW. "In many regions, JNIM effectively controls the security situation, collects taxes, mediates local conflicts and in some areas is more present than the Malian state."

Why the US is considering attacking JNIM

According to the US National Counterterrorism Center, JNIM was responsible for more than 1,200 deaths in 2025, making it the second-deadliest terrorist organization in the world. Particularly concerning is the group's geographic expansion: JNIM is now active not only in Burkina Faso and Niger, but increasingly in the coastal states of West Africa. 

The US government is divided over the question of direct military strikes. Supporters such as Sebastian Gorka, senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council, argue that JNIM is one of the world's most dangerous jihadist organizations and that its advance must be halted.

Russia's security strategy in Mali has so far failed to deliver results, according to Rüttershof. 

"After the withdrawal of French forces, the UN mission MINUSMA, and European training missions, Mali's military government argued that Russia could stabilize the security situation more effectively," Gorka told DW. "That expectation has not been fulfilled so far. On the contrary, JNIM appears stronger today than it was several years ago."

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Bamako increasingly distanced itself from Western partners and expanded cooperation with Russia.

Mali's lukewarm reaction to US potential airstrikes against jihadists

The Malian government has responded cautiously to reports of possible US airstrikes.

"We have received absolutely no confirmation from the United States," Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop said. "But I can assure you that Mali is not simply sitting and waiting for others to come and solve our problem."

Mali, he said, is relying on its own security forces and on preserving its sovereignty.

Public opinion is also divided. One resident of Bamako told DW: "Anything that ultimately brings us peace, throughout the entire territory of the country, is welcome."

Another resident pointed to the close cooperation with Russia: "Russian forces are already present on our soil, and now the Americans also want to come. Our authorities know better than anyone else what is good for the population and what harms us. I think the option of an American military intervention in Mali is not a bad idea."

Risks of escalation, more radicalization

Abdoulmoumouni Abbas, an expert on preventing radicalization in the Sahel, warns against overestimating the effectiveness of US military strikes. Experiences from US-supported counterterrorism operations in Nigeria provide important lessons. 

"The results of such operations, including those in Nigeria, raise many questions. The initial strikes actually failed to achieve their objective in northern Nigeria, in the states of Sokoto and Kebbi," Abbas told DW.

While targeted attacks could weaken JNIM's leadership structures, the underlying causes of the conflict, such as poverty, weak institutions, and ethnic tensions, would remain unresolved. Moreover, retaliation against Western interests in the region could follow.

"It becomes more problematic when military actions cause civilian casualties. Every civilian-related mistake can be exploited by JNIM for propaganda purposes and used to recruit new members", Rüttershof told DW.

In 2025, for example, the group carried out a months-long blockade of major fuel shipments to Bamako and in 2026 participated in coordinated attacks on military installations across several regions of Mali. 

Mali's geopolitical importance for the US

A US intervention would have not only security implications but also geopolitical consequences. The Sahel has become an arena of international competition. Russia has significantly expanded its influence in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger in recent years.

"If Washington were actually to take military action, this would not only be about counterterrorism," said Rüttershof. "It would also be a signal that the United States wants to remain capable of acting as a security actor."

For Mali's leaders, this would raise the question of how to navigate between the interests of external powers without losing their own political autonomy.

Foreign Minister Diop emphasized: "What we expect from a partner is that they come to Mali and ask Mali what Mali actually needs."

The conflict in Mali cannot be permanently resolved through military means alone, Rüttershof warned. In some regions, people experience the state only through corrupt security forces, while schools, healthcare and functioning courts are absent.

"JNIM exploits existing dissatisfaction. That does not necessarily mean that the population shares its ideology, but many people pragmatically choose whichever actors can provide some form of order."

For that reason, counterterrorism efforts must also include state-building, good governance, and economic development.

Saleh Mwanamilongo and Mahamadou Kane contributed to this article.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

entries.title: Why is Germany building roads for yesterday's climate?
entries.summary: As the Autobahn buckles under heat waves, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix that — so what's the holdup?
entries.content:
July 28, 2026

As the Autobahn buckles under heat waves, Germany is still paving roads for a past climate. Engineers know how to fix that — so what's the holdup?

Multi-day European heat waves with temperatures topping 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius) are increasingly leaving their mark on Germany's famed Autobahn — buckling concrete slabs, deforming asphalt and forcing temporary speed limits.

In early July alone, seven stretches of the country's highways had to be shut down completely for a time.

"The cause often lies in the bitumen — the petroleum-derived binder in asphalt. It's elastic and can soften at high temperatures, from around 60 degrees Celsius," a spokesperson from Autobahn GmbH, the company that manages Germany's highways, told DW.

Bitumen is a component in most of the country's roads.

When outdoor temperatures climb above 30 degrees Celsius, the surface of dark asphalt can quickly heat to double that or more in the sun and then deform. Using modern, bitumen-free asphalt mixes lowers the risk of such damage, according to Autobahn GmbH.

So, as heat waves intensify and traffic volumes rise, are Germany's roads built to last?

Autobahn need to be prepared for the heat

German roads are "not designed for these stresses at all," said Nina Stelzenmüller. The engineer heads the road construction technology division at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in southwestern Germany.

"The composition of the road surface is based on experience from the last 30 or 50 years," and not on the increasingly noticeable shifts in the climate, explained Stelzenmüller.

At present, road surfaces have to be designed for a temperature range of minus 30 degrees Celsius to plus 45 degrees Celsius, according to Autobahn GmbH. They are built, the company said, to withstand "the climatic stresses from heat and cold to be expected in Germany."

Yet in some regions of eastern Germany, temperatures could exceed that 45C maximum on certain days by the year 2040. That's according to climate models from Germany's National Meteorological Service (DWD), which assume emissions will remain high in the coming years and that global warming will continue to intensify.

A studyinvolving the research institute of Germany's federal transport ministry (BASt) likewise concludes that climate change is already pushing existing road materials to their limits, and that action is needed. But these findings have not yet translated into binding requirements for updating street surfaces.

Resurfacing as an opportunity: climate-ready asphalt for the future

Every road resurfaced today needs to withstand temperatures that may only become reality decades from now. But there are plenty of ways to make Germany's vital road infrastructure heat-resistant for the medium to long-term.

A 2019 study, also involving BASt, found that dark asphalt heated up by 7C less when light-colored quartzite was mixed in. The researchers recommended applying reflective surface layers to roads and building in other cooling materials as quickly as possible. The study did not examine the cost or durability of such heat adaptations.

According to Autobahn GmbH, lighter-colored stone is already being used in construction in some cases. The regional availability and cost of such stone also play a role in its use, said the company.

Individual states and cities are also testing and planning light-colored road surfaces, including in the western German cities of Oberhausen and Stuttgart, as well as the eastern state of Brandenburg.

Just scattering light-colored quartzite over the asphalt surface could also help, according to Stelzenmüller, and would be a short-term, feasible approach.

Global models: water in the asphalt and reflective coatings

Germany isn't alone in facing increasingly hot roads. Infrastructure needs to be adapted worldwide.

Tokyo, for example, already uses reflective, water-retaining road surfaces as standard when resurfacing streets. These can lower the surface temperature by 8 to 10 degrees Celsius. By 2030, some 152 miles (245 kilometers) of roads in the Japanese capital are to be fitted with them.

In Phoenix, in the US state of Arizona, light-colored coatings have also already been applied to numerous streets. They reflect more sunlight, so absorb less heat. During the day, they were around 6.7 degrees Celsius cooler than conventional surfaces. But at the same time, this noticeably warmed the ambient air for passersby.

But Germany, like many other countries, is still a long way from the systematic use of suitable road surfaces to combat heat damage. And even as average temperatures keep rising, the challenge remains that the road surface also has to stay stable in freezing winter conditions.

As an alternative to bitumen, high-performance binders that can survive both extremes — frost and heat — are currently being developed, said Stelzenmüller.

"For one thing, they're especially elastic, so that at low temperatures they can still bear the stresses caused by the cold. But at the same time they also have a very high strength, which allows them to withstand deformation at high temperatures," explained the engineer.

Policy lags behind the research

A great deal of research on climate-adapted road construction already exists, according to Stelzenmüller.

"But by the time these findings are actually written into regulation and roads are routinely built with them — that's a process that will take years if not decades. I don't expect it can be implemented in the next two or three years," she added.

The heat-ready overhaul of the infrastructure could happen faster if the transport ministry and the road-construction authorities pushed the issue. That's what happened with the tightening of pollutant limits in the development of asphalt mixes.

In 2025, Germany's transport ministry ordered that less-toxic surfaces be adopted "as quickly as possible," even before a new directive on the issue officially took effect.

"There was a real sense of urgency to meet those limits. And here it worked out [quickly], establishing new regulations within a few years," she said.

For road construction that is adapted to climate change and fit for the future, authorities need to take a similar approach, said Stelzenmüller.

"If you put a stronger focus on it, you could certainly have new types of asphalt within a few years," Stelzenmüller added.

By the time of publication, Germany's transport ministry had not responded to DW's request for comment.

This article was translated from German by Josh Axelrod.

entries.title: Japan: Strong earthquake hits Kumamoto, many feared dead
entries.summary: Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, many are feared dead after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan: Strong earthquake hits Kumamoto, many feared dead

July 28, 2026

Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, many are feared dead after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon, triggering emergency warnings and prompting authorities to assess the extent of the damage.

Japan's public broadcaster, NHK, reported that "many people" were trapped inside an Aeon shopping mall damaged by the earthquake. Earlier, local police reported an explosion at the mall in Kashima Town.

According to local broadcaster TBS, police said "quite a few" were presumed dead in the incident.

Meanwhile, NHK reported that at least 50 people were hospitalized after the earthquake.

Authorities assess damage as tsunami threat eases

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also said initial reports indicated multiple injuries, damage to civilian infrastructure, and fires in several affected areas.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she added.

Although the earthquake caused widespread disruption and temporarily raised fears of a tsunami, officials later confirmed that the threat had subsided and that Japan's coastline was no longer in danger.

"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far," a spokesperson for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. "For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions."

Power and nuclear facilities remain safe

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported that no abnormalities were detected at three nearby nuclear power plants, providing reassurance in a country still sensitive to nuclear safety concerns following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

However, the earthquake disrupted electricity supplies across the region. According to Kyushu Electric Power, approximately 45,000 households and facilities in Kumamoto temporarily lost power following the tremor.

Several major industrial facilities are located near the earthquake zone, including operations belonging to Sony and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker. Sony stated that it was evaluating conditions at its facilities, while TSMC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Japan's long history of major earthquakes

Kumamoto is no stranger to devastating seismic events.

In 2016, the region was struck by two major earthquakes, first a magnitude 6.5 quake and then a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days later. The disaster claimed 273 lives, injured more than 2,800 people. Thousands of buildings were either damaged or destroyed, making it one of Japan's most destructive recent earthquake disasters.

More recently, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck northern Japan on June 25, causing little damage and no fatalities. Earlier this year, on April 20, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in northern Japan injured at least ten people and shook high-rise buildings as far away as Tokyo, prompting authorities to issue a temporary advisory warning of an increased risk of even stronger earthquakes. That advisory was lifted a week later.

One of the world's most earthquake-prone nations

Japan sits along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most active seismic zones on Earth where four major tectonic plates meet.

Home to approximately 125 million people, the country experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year and accounts for roughly 18% of the world's seismic activity.

While most tremors are relatively minor, Japan remains haunted by memories of the catastrophic magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck the country's northeast coast in March 2011. The disaster killed or left missing around 18,500 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Tuesday's earthquake demonstrated the country's preparedness systems, emergency response capabilities, and monitoring of critical infrastructure. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi office also posted a safety guideline on X, assuring that their safety remains their top priority.

As authorities continue to assess the impact of the Kumamoto quake, residents are being urged to stay alert for potential aftershocks and follow official safety guidance.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Will Pakistan intervene amid Houthi attacks on Saudi ships?
entries.summary: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia are strategic defense partners, but experts say there are limits to how far Islamabad can go in opposing Iran-backed Houthis.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Will Pakistan intervene amid Houthi attacks on Saudi ships?

July 28, 2026

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia are strategic defense partners, but experts say there are limits to how far Islamabad can go in opposing Iran-backed Houthis.

Pakistan condemned attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea by Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi militia last week as the conflict in the Middle East threatens to expand.

In a statement, the Pakistani Foreign Ministry warned that any Houthi threat to Pakistani maritime interests in the Red Sea could be met with the "lawful use of force."

Pakistan enjoys a trade and security relationship with Saudi Arabia, and Pakistani-flagged vessels frequent Saudi ports in the Red Sea. Last September, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense agreement that contains a "collective security" clause, meaning attack on one country is considered an attack on both.

After the Houthis launched missiles at southern Saudi Arabia last week, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry expressed its "unwavering commitment" to the security pact.

At the same time, Pakistan also has ties with Iran, and has been a key mediator between Tehran and Washington to end the Iran war.

Any military act against the Iran-backed Houthis could place Islamabad in one of the most complicated foreign policy situations it has faced in years.

Pakistan's tightrope between Saudis and Iran

Historically, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have shared close military and strategic relations. Pakistani military generals and advisers have aided the kingdom for decades.

Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen expert at London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW that Pakistani troops are already in Yemen in support of the Saudis, "carrying out security and training-related duties alongside Saudi forces."

A Pakistani official DW spoke to categorically denied this claim.

Nevertheless, if Houthi attacks on oil tankers and commercial shipping escalate in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia could turn to Pakistan for help.

"Pakistan is one of Riyadh's closest defense partners, and their mutual defense pact makes such a request plausible. Having also come under Iranian attack, Saudi Arabia may increasingly look to Islamabad for military assistance if it feels under growing security pressure," Michael Kugelman, senior fellow at the Washington-based Atlantic Council, told DW.

However, Pakistan's improving ties with Iran and its mediation to end the US-Iran conflict could complicate any Pakistani military role on Saudi Arabia's behalf. 

"Pakistan and Iran have a complicated relationship based on the calculation of tactical gains by either side. In any case, Pakistan has warned Iran several times that in case of conflict it will support Saudi Arabia," Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani military analyst and senior fellow at King's College London, told DW.

After a period of unprecedented tensions in 2024, when Iran and Pakistan exchanged cross-border missile strikes, the neighbors have since rebuilt diplomatic relations and strengthened cooperation against militant groups operating along their shared border.

"Limited military support for Saudi Arabia would not necessarily rupture Pakistan's ties with Iran. But at a time when Islamabad is trying to present itself as a neutral mediator, expanding arms support to Riyadh could deepen Tehran's suspicions and undermine Pakistan's diplomatic role," Kugelman said.

How much support can Pakistan give?

If Saudi Arabia seeks assistance, analysts say Pakistan's contribution would most likely focus on protecting Saudi interests rather than joining offensive operations.

"The preference would be for defensive engagement, as expanding operations in the Red Sea may prove too risky," said Siddiqa.

Such an approach could include intelligence sharing, air-defense cooperation, maritime surveillance and protecting critical Saudi infrastructure, allowing Pakistan to support Riyadh without joining offensive operations.

"Despite its deep military ties and mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan is unlikely to provide arms or troops. Islamabad is focused on preventing regional escalation and preserving its role as a mediator in the Iran conflict, making any military support for Riyadh politically risky and potentially damaging to its ties with Tehran," said Kugelman.

Will Saudi Arabia escalate?

Saudi Arabia has exercised considerable restraint since winding down its large-scale military campaign in Yemen. However, repeated attacks on oil infrastructure and commercial shipping may eventually force Riyadh to respond more aggressively.

"Continued Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels could prompt Riyadh to abandon its restraint and launch a military response," said Al-Muslimi.

King's College analyst Siddiqa said it is not clear that Saudi Arabia currently has the capacity to fight a prolonged sub-conventional war against the Houthis.

"While it may intensify air strikes, more bombardment alone is unlikely to achieve the objective of making the kingdom more secure," she said.

The analysts agreed Islamabad will likely back maritime security and freedom of navigation while avoiding direct strikes on Houthi targets amid the looming US-Iran conflict. But if the Red Sea conflict escalates, staying neutral may become increasingly difficult as pressure from Riyadh and Tehran grows.

"The trajectory of the conflict with Iran will shape Saudi Arabia's tolerance for Houthi attacks," said Kugelman.

"If the current pause between the US and Iran holds, Riyadh is likely to wait out the attacks rather than escalate. But Saudi Arabia will continue to view Pakistan as a key security partner because Houthi attacks are unlikely to stop, even if the Iran conflict ends," he added.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany: Online tourist accommodation bookings hit new peak
entries.summary: Vacation rental bookings through online platforms have climbed to a new record in Germany. The figures reveal major regional differences in where certain tourists like to go.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Online tourist accommodation bookings hit new peak

July 28, 2026

Vacation rental bookings through online platforms have climbed to a new record in Germany. The figures reveal major regional differences in where certain tourists like to go.

Bookings for tourist accommodation in Germany through major online platforms have reached a record high.

The figure rose sharply above both last year's level and figures seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Why are tourist rental bookings rising in Germany?

Travellers booked 68.3 million overnight stays through Airbnb, Booking.com and Expedia in 2025, the Federal Statistical Office said on Tuesday, citing data from EU statistics agency Eurostat.

That was an increase of 13% compared with 2024 and more than 83% above the level recorded in 2019.

The rise came despite TripAdvisor no longer being included in the data after it left the short-term accommodation booking market.

Strong domestic demand was the main driver of growth. German travellers booked 48.5 million overnight stays, an increase of more than 15% from the previous year.

The number of domestic bookings has more than doubled since 2019.

Foreign visitors booked 19.8 million overnight stays, almost 8% more than in 2024.

Who is visiting Germany's tourist spots?

Travellers from the Netherlands accounted for the largest number of international bookings, with 2.9 million overnight stays, followed by Poland with 2.1 million and the US with 1.3 million.

The figures largely reflect the market for smaller and privately operated accommodation.

Around 94% of booked nights were spent at properties with fewer than 10 beds, which are not included in Germany's official monthly tourism statistics.

The platform data therefore provide a broader picture of the country's short-term accommodation market.

Bavaria recorded the highest number of overnight stays, with 10.6 million. Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia followed with 8.1 million each.

Travel patterns varied considerably between Germany's states.

Around 90% of guests in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Schleswig-Holstein came from within Germany, while city-states and western regions attracted a larger share of international visitors.

Foreign guests accounted for more than two-thirds of bookings in Berlin, at 67.7%.

Their share was also above average in North Rhine-Westphalia, at 42.3%, and Baden-Württemberg, at 40.8%.
